newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico sterling bond to refinance short-term debt.
newsitem.headline: Mexico sterling bond to refinance short-term debt.

text.p: Mexico's finance ministry said on Wednesday that it will use the proceeds of its five-year 300 million sterling Eurobond to refinance short-term debt.
"In accordance with the public debt policies established at the start of the year, the funds from this placement will be used to refinance short-term obligations," the ministry said in a release.
The Eurobond, launched Wednesday and worth about $480 million, will pay an annual yield of 8.75 percent, or 173 basis points over five-year U.S. Treasuries.
It was the first sterling bond issued in more than five years by the Mexican federal government, formally known as the United Mexican States (UMS).
The last UMS sterling bond issue, placed in November 1991, was a 100 million sterling seven-year bond. In 1981, the UMS also placed a 50 million sterling issue.
Mexican development bank Bancomext issued a seven-year sterling bond in 1993. Mexican state-owned oil monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) issued a 10-year sterling bond that year as well.
Since returning to debt markets after the peso crash in 1994, the UMS has steadily built yield curves in Italian lira, Japanese yen, marks, as well as U.S. dollars.
The issues it has placed so far this year have allowed it to cover its maturing market debt in 1997, valued at about $1.4 billion.

But the government also bought back its outstanding Aztec Brady bonds, and has been paying back some of what it owes to the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The federal government made a $590 million payment earlier this year.
Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz said in early May the country owes the IMF about $10.0 billion and expects to pay back $500 million more this year.
